title: Number of Pairs Satisfying Inequality
statement: You get two integer arrays `nums1` and `nums2` of the same length `n` (indexed from 0) and an integer `diff`. Count the index pairs `(i, j)` with `0 <= i < j <= n - 1` for which `nums1[i] - nums1[j]` is at most `nums2[i] - nums2[j] + diff`, and return that count.
signature: long numberOfPairs(int[] nums1, int[] nums2, int diff)
notes:
## Intuition

Checking every pair is O(n²). Move all the `i` terms to one side and the `j` terms to the other: the rule becomes `nums1[i] - nums2[i] <= nums1[j] - nums2[j] + diff`. With `value = nums1[k] - nums2[k]` for each index, every `j` asks one question: how many earlier indices have a value no larger than its own value plus `diff`? A Fenwick tree (binary indexed tree) that counts the values seen so far answers that prefix question in O(log V).

## Approach

1. Values lie in `[-20000, 20000]`, so shift them by `OFFSET = 20001` into tree positions `1..size` with `size = 40001`.
2. Scan `j` from left to right and compute `value`.
3. Query the tree for the count of stored values up to `value + diff` (clamped to `size`; a position below 1 counts nothing) and add it to `pairs`.
4. Insert `value` into the tree so later indices can pair with it.
5. Return `pairs`.

## Example 1, step by step

`value` per index is `[3-2, 2-2, 5-1] = [1, 0, 4]` and `diff = 1`. At `j = 0` the tree is empty, then `1` is added. At `j = 1` the limit is `0 + 1 = 1`; one stored value (`1`) fits, so `pairs = 1`, then `0` is added. At `j = 2` the limit is `5`; both `1` and `0` fit, so `pairs = 3`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log V), where V = 40001 is the range of shifted values.
- Space: O(V) for the tree.

## Pitfalls

- `value + diff` can go beyond the stored range in either direction; clamp the top and let a non-positive position count nothing.
- Query before inserting the current value, or each index pairs with itself.
- The count can reach about n²/2, which overflows a 32-bit integer in Java or C.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `OFFSET` | shift that maps value -20000 to tree position 1 |
| `size` | number of tree positions |
| `tree` | Fenwick tree counting stored values |
| `value` | `nums1[j] - nums2[j]` |
| `index` | current tree position while querying or updating |
| `pairs` | number of valid pairs found so far |

narration.3: Positions 1 to 40001 cover every value from -20000 to 20000.
narration.4: The Fenwick tree starts empty: no values stored yet.
narration.5: pairs counts the valid (i, j) pairs found so far.
narration.7: Treat each index in turn as j, the right end of a pair.
narration.8: After rearranging, each index is described by nums1[j] - nums2[j].
narration.9: Earlier values up to value + diff qualify; clamp the position to the top of the tree.
narration.10: Walk down the tree to sum the counts of all stored values at or below that limit.
narration.11: Add this node's count of stored values to the answer.
narration.12: Drop the lowest set bit to jump to the next prefix block.
narration.14: Now store the current value so later indices can pair with it.
narration.15: Walk up the tree through every node that covers this position.
narration.16: Each covering node counts one more value.
narration.17: Add the lowest set bit to move to the next covering node.
narration.20: Every index has been matched against all earlier ones; return the total.
